newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa frees individuals to invest offshore.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa frees individuals to invest offshore.

text.p: Private South African individuals will be allowed to invest up to 200,000 ($44,440) overseas from July 1, the Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday.
The move, which will allow residents to invest directly in foreign markets for the first time, marks the latest step in the government's programme of gradually rolling down exchange controls.

The ministry said that the higher-than-expected allowance could be seen as a further indication of its commitment to the liberalisation of exchange controls as fast as economic circumstances permitted.
Officials had indicated earlier that the limit was likely to be set at around 160,000 rand, equivalent to the travel allowance for a married couple.

The initial allowance could be held offshore or alternatively in foreign currency deposits with domestic foreign exchange dealers, it said in a statement. South African residents will be allowed to retain abroad income derived from foreign sources.

At the same time, individuals will be allowed to apply to the exchange control department of the Reserve Bank to invest in fixed property, such as holiday homes and farms in Southern African Development Community member states from July 1.

"I believe that these measures will boost confidence, both domestically and internationally, in the South African economy and lay the foundations for the further liberalisation of the remaining exchange controls in the future," said Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.
To qualify for the latest relaxation in capital controls, residents will have to sign a declaration of good standing in respect of their South African tax obligations.
Uncertainty about the impact of the July 1 relaxation has dominated trading in South Africa's financial markets recently.

Investors are nervous that the move could trigger an outflow of capital, although a build-up in official reserves to record levels and the negotiation of foreign credit lines has convinced many that Pretoria is well-equipped to stand such a shock.

Official reserves stood at 21.8 billion rand at the end of May, having surged from 14.4 billion in April on the back of inflows from the sale of 30 percent of state telecommunication concern Telkom and continued foreign purchases of bonds and shares.
The ministry noted that institutional investors had already invested 27.7 billion rand abroad to date under earlier liberalisation measures.
